_: Short notes shown on a piece's page in the library, keyed by catalogue id. Only well-documented facts; say so when a story is a legend. tools/catalog/publish.js copies them into dist/library/catalog.json as `about`.
chopin/op-28/15: The nickname isn't Chopin's. It comes from George Sand's memoir of the winter of 1838–39, which the two spent in a former monastery at Valldemossa on Majorca. She describes coming home through a storm to find him playing a prelude he had just written, convinced he had dreamed of drowning while drops of water fell on his chest. Which prelude she meant is uncertain, but the A♭ that repeats through this one, written as G♯ in its dark middle section, kept the name here.
chopin/op-28/4: One of the two preludes played on the organ of the Madeleine in Paris at Chopin's funeral in 1849, together with the sixth.
beethoven/op-27-no-2: Beethoven called it Sonata quasi una fantasia, a sonata in the manner of a fantasy, because it opens with a slow movement instead of a fast one. The name “Moonlight” came after his death, from the critic Ludwig Rellstab, who likened the first movement to moonlight over Lake Lucerne. Beethoven dedicated it to his pupil Countess Giulietta Guicciardi.
beethoven/woo-59: Für Elise was never published in Beethoven's lifetime. The scholar Ludwig Nohl printed it in 1867 from an autograph that has since been lost, so no one can check how he read the dedication. Who Elise was is still debated: one theory is that Nohl misread “Therese”, for Therese Malfatti, whom Beethoven hoped to marry around 1810.
beethoven/op-13: One of the few nicknames Beethoven approved of: the sonata was published in 1799 as the Grande sonate pathétique. The slow introduction comes back twice inside the fast first movement, which was unusual at the time.
beethoven/op-57: Like “Moonlight”, the name is not Beethoven's: a Hamburg publisher put “Appassionata” on an edition in 1838, eleven years after his death. Beethoven wrote it in 1804–05, and his pupil Carl Czerny said he thought it his greatest sonata until the “Hammerklavier”.
chopin/op-66: Chopin wrote it in 1834 and never published it. After his death his friend Julian Fontana brought it out in 1855, against Chopin's wish that his unpublished manuscripts be destroyed, and it was Fontana who added “Fantaisie” to the title.
chopin/op-10/12: Chopin finished his first set of études around 1831, the year the Russian army crushed the November Uprising and took Warsaw while he was abroad. This one's storm of left-hand runs has been linked with that news ever since, though the name “Revolutionary” is not his.
chopin/op-23: Chopin's first ballade, published in 1836. Schumann wrote that when he told Chopin it was his favourite of all his works, Chopin answered after a long pause that it was his own favourite too.
chopin/op-64/1: “Minute” means small, not sixty seconds: played well it takes closer to two minutes. Its French nickname, Valse du petit chien, comes from the story that George Sand's little dog chasing its tail gave Chopin the idea.
chopin/op-53: The polonaise, a stately Polish court dance, became an emblem of home for Chopin, who left Poland at twenty and never returned. This one, from 1842, is the grandest of them, with a middle section of thundering left-hand octaves.
chopin/op-9/2: Chopin's best-loved nocturne, written when he was about twenty. The nocturne was the invention of the Irish pianist John Field; Chopin took the form and gave its melody the ornate turns of the Italian opera he loved.
debussy/l-75/3: The title comes from Paul Verlaine's poem “Clair de lune”, whose moonlit masked dancers belong to the same imagined eighteenth-century world as the suite's other movements. Debussy began the Suite bergamasque around 1890 but published it only in 1905, after revising it.
rachmaninoff/op-3/2: Rachmaninoff was nineteen when he first played it in public, in 1892. He sold it with the rest of his Op. 3 to his publisher for a single fee, and because Russia had not signed the international copyright agreements, the countless editions printed abroad earned him nothing.
liszt/s-141/3: Liszt built it on the final rondo of Paganini's Second Violin Concerto, where a little bell (campanella) rings along with the tune. The high repeated D♯ and the right hand's leaps of more than two octaves are Liszt's bell.
liszt/s-244-2: The best known of Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies, built like a Hungarian verbunkos: a slow, brooding lassan, then a wild friska. In 1946 and 1947 it starred in two cartoons, played by Bugs Bunny in Rhapsody Rabbit and by Tom in the Oscar-winning The Cat Concerto.
liszt/s-541/3: Liszt first wrote the three Liebesträume (dreams of love) as songs, then arranged them for piano in 1850. This, the third, sets Ferdinand Freiligrath's poem “O lieb, so lang du lieben kannst” (love as long as you can love).
liszt/s-139/4: Mazeppa follows Victor Hugo's poem about a young page tied to the back of a wild horse and carried across the steppe. Liszt later turned the same music into a symphonic poem for orchestra.
bach/bwv-988: Bach published it in 1741 as the fourth part of his Clavier-Übung (keyboard practice): an aria, thirty variations on its bass line, and the aria again. Every third variation is a canon, each at a wider interval than the last. The story that it was written for the harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg to play to a count who could not sleep comes from Bach's first biographer and is doubted.
bach/bwv-846-869/1/1: The first prelude of The Well-Tempered Clavier, which Bach completed in 1722: twenty-four preludes and fugues, one in every major and minor key. In the 1850s Charles Gounod laid a melody over it to make his Ave Maria.
mozart/k-331/3: The “Turkish” rondo imitates the Janissary bands of the Ottoman army, whose drums, cymbals and triangles were the height of fashion in Vienna. The whole sonata is unusual: none of its three movements is in sonata form, and it opens with a set of variations.
mozart/k-545: Mozart entered it in his catalogue in June 1788 as a little keyboard sonata for beginners, and generations of piano students have known it as the Sonata facile, the easy sonata.
schumann/op-15/7: Träumerei (dreaming) is the seventh of Schumann's thirteen Scenes from Childhood, written in 1838. Schumann said they were not pieces for children but a grown-up's memories of childhood, for grown-ups.
schubert/d-899/3: Schubert wrote it in G♭ major, a key with six flats. When Tobias Haslinger published it in 1857, almost thirty years after Schubert's death, he moved it to G major, and editions kept the easier key for decades.
tchaikovsky/op-37a: Commissioned by the Saint Petersburg magazine Nouvellist, which printed one piece a month through 1876, each headed by a few lines of Russian poetry.
grieg/op-65/6: Grieg wrote it for his and Nina's silver wedding anniversary in 1892. Troldhaugen (troll hill) was their home outside Bergen, where the two are buried in the cliff above the lake.
